title: Layla and Majnun
hookLine: Nizami's tale: Qays loves Layla to madness, and Sufis read it as longing for God

cards: A boy named Qays sits in a schoolroom and can't stop looking at a girl named Layla. She looks back. By the time the grown-ups notice, it's too late: he's composing poems about her, out loud, in the street.
People start calling him by a new name, Majnun, the one who has lost his mind. The story was told in Arabic poetry and retold by the Persian poet Nizami, and poets kept retelling it after him.

teach.b: In Nizami's telling, Layla's family keep her away from Qays, and her father refuses the marriage. She is married to another man.
Qays goes into the wilderness, lives among wild animals, and sings his poems to her across the sand. The two never really live together, and both die still apart. But it isn't only a tragedy.

Sufis, the mystics of Islam, read Majnun as a picture of the soul. A lover who gives up reputation, comfort and good sense for one beloved looks, to them, like the seeker who gives up everything for God.

Layla becomes a sign of the divine beauty the soul is looking for. Rumi adds a moment in his Masnavi. A caliph asks to see the well-known Layla, looks her over and shrugs: you're no more beautiful than other women.
Layla answers, in effect: be quiet, you are not Majnun. Beauty lives in the lover's eyes; to someone outside, the beloved seems ordinary.
It's a love so complete that ordinary sense can't contain it, and Sufi poets return to that image: to love God fully may look foolish from outside.
The story keeps both readings: a boy and a girl who loved and lost, and a soul that won't stop looking for what it loves.

how: The story of Layla and Majnun is told and sung across the Muslim world, and Sufi poets and teachers use Majnun as an image of the lover of God who gives up everything for the Beloved.

games.q: you're Layla. the caliph looks you over and says, you're no more beautiful than other women. what do you say?
o: be quiet: you are not Majnun.
games.why: in Rumi's telling, Layla answers that he isn't Majnun. beauty lives in the eyes of the lover.

practice: Find an old love letter, a card or a message from someone who loved you, or whom you loved, or bring one back from memory.

Read it slowly, without judging how it ended, and notice only how the words looked at the other person: what they saw that nobody else saw. If you pray, you can bring that longing into your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Majnun. The name given to Qays for his love of Layla, read by Sufis as the soul's own longing for God. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: one who has lost his mind, the name people gave Qays.
